                    ### Question
                    A 12-year-old female with no past medical history is found to have an abnormal cardiovascular exam during routine physical examination at her pediatrician’s office. All other components of her physical exam are normal. During evaluation for potential causes for her abnormal exam, an echocardiogram with doppler is done that shows flow between the atria. Which of the following would would have most likely been auscultated as a result of the pathology on her echocardiogram?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Increased splitting of S1 with inspiration
opb. Decreased splitting of S1 with inspiration
opc. Normal splitting of S2
opd. Increased splitting of S2 with inspiration
ope. Splitting of S2 in inspiration and expiration

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The abnormal cardiovascular exam and echocardiogram findings indicating flow between the atria suggest the presence of an atrial septal defect (ASD) or a patent foramen ovale (PFO). Both conditions can lead to increased blood flow to the right atrium, resulting in increased right heart volume and workload. This hemodynamic change typically causes increased splitting of S2 with inspiration due to enhanced right ventricular stroke volume and prolonged right ventricular ejection time. The reasoning chains correctly identify this outcome, aligning with standard medical consensus. Evidence paths related to echocardiography and atrial septal defects support the conclusion that increased splitting of S2 with inspiration is the most likely auscultation finding in this scenario.
